label: Battery acid
summary: Lead-acid batteries hold sulphuric acid that burns skin and eyes and eats clothing and metal. When charging, and especially when overcharged, they give off hydrogen, which explodes from a single spark.
signs: White, grey or blue crust on the terminals or the tray
Wet, sticky or stained case, or a puddle under the battery
Rotten-egg smell near a battery on charge: it is being overcharged
Holes in clothing or rust spots on metal around old batteries
do: Wear eye protection whenever you handle a lead-acid battery
Keep the battery upright when you carry it
Keep a bucket of clean water and a box of baking soda nearby
Neutralise spills on the ground or on tools with baking soda and water until the fizzing stops, then rinse
Charge in a ventilated space, away from sparks and flames
Connect the charger clips before switching the charger on; switch it off before you take them off
On a vehicle, take the earth lead (the one bolted to the body or engine) off first and put it back last; on almost all vehicles that is the negative
dont: Don't lean over the battery while connecting or disconnecting anything
Don't smoke, grind or use flames near batteries on charge
Don't charge a battery that is frozen, cracked or bulging
Don't let a wrench or other metal bridge the terminals: it can weld on and throw molten metal
Don't put baking soda in eyes or on skin: use plain water
ppe: Indirect-vent goggles, with a face shield over them when pouring or filling
Rubber or nitrile gloves for battery acid; butyl or neoprene for strong acids; hydrofluoric acid needs gloves made for it
An apron and long sleeves, ideally old clothes you don’t mind losing
firstAid: Acid on skin: rinse with plenty of clean water for at least 30 minutes (CCOHS, for battery acid) and take off soaked clothing
Acid in an eye: rinse with clean running water for at least 30 minutes (CCOHS, for battery acid), holding the lids open, then get medical help
Swallowed acid: rinse the mouth; if they are fully awake and can swallow, give a few small sips of water or milk; don't make them vomit and don't give baking soda; get medical help
Burns that blister, are wider than about 5–8 cm (2–3 in), or involve the eyes need real medical care
